aic:46450.texto:
Ren Yi was among the most successful and influential among Chinese painters of the so-called Shanghai School. Arriving in Shanghai in 1857, he took the artistic name “bonian” (one-hundred years), claiming that it would take him a century to achieve success. However, by 1875 Ren Yi was the best-known painter in Shanghai. His highly sought-after bird-and-flower paintings initially followed the Song dynasty (960–1279) convention of applying rich color fields within outlines, producing decorative patterning with lifelike representation. This work represents his mature, more spontaneous style that is characterized by looser brushwork, more ink washes, and greater tonal variation.
The contrast between the delicate flowers and thick vines of the wisteria make this plant ideal for showcasing an artist’s calligraphic prowess. In this painting, Ren Yi demonstrates his impressive range of brush techniques: dry, rough strokes dragged across the paper compose the wisteria vines; wet jumbles of short strokes imbue volume to the rocks; and subtle gradations of color dotted on the paper form the wisteria flowers. In the center sits a pair of paradise flycatchers. Their Chinese name, shoudai niao (sash bird), which describes the species’ long ribbonlike tails, is a homophone for the term shou (longevity). By combining a vibrant palette of colors, some of which were imported from Europe, with the bravado of his monochromatic brush technique, Ren Yi imbued past traditions with fresh innovation.
aic:46450.title: Paradise Flycatchers and Wisteria

cma:132908.texto:
Similar to some calligraphers of his time, Zhu Da rejected conventions in favor of an individual, personal expression. He is known for ambiguous compositions of fish, flowers, birds, and rocks in contrasting ink tonality. As a member of the Ming imperial family, Zhu lost his princely status and hid in a monastery when the Manchus, foreigners from the north, established the Qing dynasty in 1644.

In this late work, mountain ranges are rendered in diverse and dense strokes rising toward the top of the scroll. It references the artist Dong Qichang (1555–1636) in concept. Yet the cursory brushwork and composition present Zhu’s personal style.
cma:132908.title: Landscape after Guo Zhongshu

cma:132908.texto: Zhu Da's inscription acknowledges that this painting was done after the early Song master Guo Zhongshu 郭忠恕, but there is almost no tangible stylistic relation to be found between Zhu Da and his 10th-century model.
cma:132908.title: Landscape after Guo Zhongshu

cma:147906.texto:
The plum flourishes in the mild climate of the south, and it was not before the Six Dynasties period (220– 589 CE) that the motif began to be appreciated by southern artists, many of whom had emigrated from the north. 

Wang Mian from Zhejiang province had failed the civil and military service examinations and later rejected appointments under the Mongol government. Instead, he chose to return home, making a living by selling plum paintings. Few of Wang’s works have survived, but they demonstrate that by his time the ink-plum (momei) genre was fully developed.
cma:147906.title: A Prunus in the Moonlight

cma:147906.texto: The painting portrays the plum in the nighttime, as indicated by the tint of the background and the presence of the moon.

cma:149625.texto:
The twenty paintings in this double-album by Chen Hongshou include landscapes, figures, and flowers. It also has one leaf featuring a woman, an often-used subject not found in the other albums from the latter part of his career. His late works are wonderful summations of Chen's peculiar and quirky art--archaistic, hyper-refined--but without accompanying shallowness or sentimentality.

His figures and landscapes in the late albums are miniaturized, not unlike the small Chinese gardens, or the carefully selected small table rocks or old roots used for contemplation to see the world in miniature. This loss of scale is quite deliberate and reflects the psychological situation of a depressed class like the Ming loyalist officials and scholars, deprived of their integrity and honor, and forced to lead a diminished and restricted existence.
cma:149625.title: Paintings after Ancient Masters: An Ancient Tree

cma:160133.texto:
The flower-and-bird subjects here are depicted in a meticulous manner, echoing the academic tradition but translating the customarily colored images to plain monochrome. Fine ink lines combined with carefully graded washes define the contours and give subtle modeling to the natural forms. 

Wang Yuan excelled in flower-and-bird subjects as well as landscape and figure paintings. A child prodigy, he was instructed by the great Yuan master Zhao Mengfu at an early age.
cma:160133.title: Quails and Sparrows in an Autumn Scene

referencias.texto_citado:
Ren Yi was among the most successful and influential among Chinese painters of the so-called Shanghai School. Arriving in Shanghai in 1857, he took the artistic name “bonian” (one-hundred years), claiming that it would take him a century to achieve success. However, by 1875 Ren Yi was the best-known painter in Shanghai. His highly sought-after bird-and-flower paintings initially followed the Song dynasty (960–1279) convention of applying rich color fields within outlines, producing decorative patterning with lifelike representation. This work represents his mature, more spontaneous style that is characterized by looser brushwork, more ink washes, and greater tonal variation.
The contrast between the delicate flowers and thick vines of the wisteria make this plant ideal for showcasing an artist’s calligraphic prowess. In this painting, Ren Yi demonstrates his impressive range of brush techniques: dry, rough strokes dragged across the paper compose the wisteria vines; wet jumbles of short strokes imbue volume to the rocks; and subtle gradations of color dotted on the paper form the wisteria flowers. In the center sits a pair of paradise flycatchers. Their Chinese name, shoudai niao (sash bird), which describes the species’ long ribbonlike tails, is a homophone for the term shou (longevity). By combining a vibrant palette of colors, some of which were imported from Europe, with the bravado of his monochromatic brush technique, Ren Yi imbued past traditions with fresh innovation.

1. **Quails and Sparrows in an Autumn Scene**
   Wang Yuan · 1347 · hanging scroll, ink on paper
   Ficha oficial: https://clevelandart.org/art/1997.91

   La obra representa un tema de flores y pájaros, un motivo tradicional en la pintura china. [1]
   La técnica utiliza tinta monocromática con líneas finas y lavados graduados para definir las formas naturales, lo que es característico de la pintura china clásica.

   **Fuentes**
   [1] “The flower-and-bird subjects here are depicted in a meticulous manner, echoing the academic tradition but translating the customarily colored images to plain monochrome. Fine ink lines combined with carefully graded washes define the contours and give subtle modeling to the natural forms. 

Wang Yuan excelled in flower-and-bird subjects as well as landscape and figure paintings. A child prodigy, he was instructed by the great Yuan master Zhao Mengfu at an early age.”
       https://clevelandart.org/art/1997.91 · CC0 1.0

2. **Paintings after Ancient Masters: An Ancient Tree**
   Chen Hongshou · 1598–1652 · album leaf, ink and color on silk
   Ficha oficial: https://clevelandart.org/art/1979.27.2.20

   Incluye pinturas de flores entre otros temas, dentro de un álbum que refleja la tradición china de miniaturas y temas contemplativos. [1]
   El enfoque en flores y la miniaturización del tema es coherente con la tradición china de representar la naturaleza en formatos pequeños para la contemplación.
   No se menciona explícitamente un tema de flores y pájaros como en la obra original, por lo que no se puede afirmar que trate el mismo tema.

   **Fuentes**
   [1] “The twenty paintings in this double-album by Chen Hongshou include landscapes, figures, and flowers. It also has one leaf featuring a woman, an often-used subject not found in the other albums from the latter part of his career. His late works are wonderful summations of Chen's peculiar and quirky art--archaistic, hyper-refined--but without accompanying shallowness or sentimentality.

His figures and landscapes in the late albums are miniaturized, not unlike the small Chinese gardens, or the carefully selected small table rocks or old roots used for contemplation to see the world in miniature. This loss of scale is quite deliberate and reflects the psychological situation of a depressed class like the Ming loyalist officials and scholars, deprived of their integrity and honor, and forced to lead a diminished and restricted existence.”
       https://clevelandart.org/art/1979.27.2.20 · CC0 1.0

3. **A Prunus in the Moonlight**
   Wang Mian · 1300s · Hanging scroll; ink on silk
   Ficha oficial: https://clevelandart.org/art/1974.26

   La obra representa un ciruelo, un motivo tradicional en la pintura china de flores y naturaleza. [1]
   La pintura muestra el ciruelo en la noche, un tema naturalista que es común en la pintura china clásica. [2]
   El uso de tinta sobre seda y la representación detallada del árbol son características típicas de la pintura china.

   **Fuentes**
   [1] “The plum flourishes in the mild climate of the south, and it was not before the Six Dynasties period (220– 589 CE) that the motif began to be appreciated by southern artists, many of whom had emigrated from the north. 

Wang Mian from Zhejiang province had failed the civil and military service examinations and later rejected appointments under the Mongol government. Instead, he chose to return home, making a living by selling plum paintings. Few of Wang’s works have survived, but they demonstrate that by his time the ink-plum (momei) genre was fully developed.”
       https://clevelandart.org/art/1974.26 · CC0 1.0
   [2] “The painting portrays the plum in the nighttime, as indicated by the tint of the background and the presence of the moon.”
       https://clevelandart.org/art/1974.26 · CC0 1.0

4. **Landscape after Guo Zhongshu**
   Bada Shanren · c. 1680–1705 · Hanging scroll; ink on paper
   Ficha oficial: https://clevelandart.org/art/1955.36

   La obra incluye elementos como peces, flores, pájaros y rocas, que son temas tradicionales en la pintura china. [1]
   El estilo personal y expresivo con tinta en papel es una variante dentro de la tradición china, aunque con una interpretación más libre.
   No se menciona que la obra trate específicamente el tema de flores y pájaros en el sentido tradicional, sino que es una interpretación personal del artista.

   **Fuentes**
   [1] “Similar to some calligraphers of his time, Zhu Da rejected conventions in favor of an individual, personal expression. He is known for ambiguous compositions of fish, flowers, birds, and rocks in contrasting ink tonality. As a member of the Ming imperial family, Zhu lost his princely status and hid in a monastery when the Manchus, foreigners from the north, established the Qing dynasty in 1644.

In this late work, mountain ranges are rendered in diverse and dense strokes rising toward the top of the scroll. It references the artist Dong Qichang (1555–1636) in concept. Yet the cursory brushwork and composition present Zhu’s personal style.”
       https://clevelandart.org/art/1955.36 · CC0 1.0

5. **Paradise Flycatchers and Wisteria**
   Ren Yi · Qing dynasty (1644–1911), 1892 · Hanging scroll; ink and colors on paper · Chinese (culture or style)
   Ficha oficial: https://www.artic.edu/artworks/46450

   La obra representa pájaros paraíso y glicinas, un tema de flores y pájaros muy tradicional en la pintura china. [1]
   El uso de tinta y color, junto con técnicas de pincel variadas, refleja la tradición china de representar la naturaleza con riqueza técnica y simbólica. [1]
   La combinación de motivos florales y aves con simbolismo de longevidad es un tema recurrente en la pintura china clásica.

   **Fuentes**
   [1] “Ren Yi was among the most successful and influential among Chinese painters of the so-called Shanghai School. Arriving in Shanghai in 1857, he took the artistic name “bonian” (one-hundred years), claiming that it would take him a century to achieve success. However, by 1875 Ren Yi was the best-known painter in Shanghai. His highly sought-after bird-and-flower paintings initially followed the Song dynasty (960–1279) convention of applying rich color fields within outlines, producing decorative patterning with lifelike representation. This work represents his mature, more spontaneous style that is characterized by looser brushwork, more ink washes, and greater tonal variation.
The contrast between the delicate flowers and thick vines of the wisteria make this plant ideal for showcasing an artist’s calligraphic prowess. In this painting, Ren Yi demonstrates his impressive range of brush techniques: dry, rough strokes dragged across the paper compose the wisteria vines; wet jumbles of short strokes imbue volume to the rocks; and subtle gradations of color dotted on the paper form the wisteria flowers. In the center sits a pair of paradise flycatchers. Their Chinese name, shoudai niao (sash bird), which describes the species’ long ribbonlike tails, is a homophone for the term shou (longevity). By combining a vibrant palette of colors, some of which were imported from Europe, with the bravado of his monochromatic brush technique, Ren Yi imbued past traditions with fresh innovation.”
       https://www.artic.edu/artworks/46450 · CC BY 4.0
       “Paradise Flycatchers and Wisteria”, Ren Yi. Art Institute of Chicago. Texto bajo CC BY 4.0 — https://www.artic.edu/artworks/46450
